abstract: Recent advances in molecular science have significantly enlightened our mechanistic understanding of spinocerebellar ataxia type 7. To further close remaining gaps, we performed a multi-omics analysis using SCA7 266Q/5Q mice. Entire brain tissue samples were collected from 12-week-old mice, and RNA sequencing, methylation analysis, and proteomic analysis were performed. Results were integrated to identify genes with identical trends in expression across all three analyses. Data from RNA sequencing and methylation analysis revealed 58 significantly hypomethylated-upregulated genes and 62 hypermethylated-downregulated genes, mostly enriched in GO terms of regulation of axonogenesis, channel activity, and monoamine signaling. In the proteomic analysis, 211 upregulated and 281 downregulated DEPs associated mostly with immune response and cellular mobility were identified. Two genes, Fam107b and Tph2 , showed differential expressions in both transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Findings were validated in RT-qPCR as well as open data source analysis. Our study is the first to perform multi-omics analysis in SCA7 mice and will serve as an important reference for future studies.
methods:
Materials and methods
The SCA7 mouse model
The SCA7
266Q/5Q
mice used in this study carry a 266 CAG repeat knockin in the exon 3 of the
Atxn7
locus, and replicate well the clinical features of infantile SCA7 (JAX stock no. 008682).
33
For healthy controls, B6.129S1 WT littermates were used. All procedures in animal handling were conducted with the approval of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Seoul National University Hospital (no. 22-0035-S1A1).
Behavioral tests
As behavioral tests, average stride length measurement and rotarod tests were performed. Twelve SCA7 mice (male = 6, female = 6) and 7 WT mice (male = 3, female = 4) were tested at weeks 7, 9, and 11 after birth. For average stride length measurement, each mouse performed two trials for every measurement period, and the average length of three strides was calculated. For the rotarod test, mice underwent four trials each on three sequential days for every measurement time point. For each trial, rotation speed was accelerated from 4 to 50 rpm, and trials were separated by 10 min each. The average latency to fall was measured and analyzed as the index parameter. All procedures were performed according to standardized protocols by experienced researchers. Statistical analysis was performed using the Student’s t test for difference in stride length, and we used multiple unpaired t tests for latency to fall in the rotarod test, correcting for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Šídák method. The overall procedure is depicted in
Figure 1
A.
Total RNA extraction, library preparation, and sequencing
Tissue collection of entire brain (including cerebrum and cerebellum) was performed on 24 mice at week 12 (
n
= 12 per group). Entire brain was selected as the target for analysis, considering that the cortex and brainstem are also regions significantly affected in SCA7,
33
and to obtain an overview of the genes that have the most general impact in overall pathogenesis. Twelve samples were created by pooling two samples from mice of matching genotype and sex. Pooling of samples was conducted to compensate for potential within-group variability.
34
,
35
Total brain RNA was extracted using QIAzol Lysis Reagent (Qiagen, Crawley, UK) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The total RNA concentration was calculated by Quant-IT RiboGreen (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, catalog no.
R11490
). To assess the integrity of the total RNA, samples were run on the TapeStation RNA screentape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, catalog no. 5067-5576). Only high-quality RNA preparations, with RNA integrity number >7.0, were used for RNA library construction. A library was independently prepared with 1 μg total RNA for each sample by Illumina TruSeq Stranded mRNA Sample Prep Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, catalog no. 20020595). The libraries were quantified using KAPA Library Quantification kits for Illumina sequencing platforms according to the qPCR Quantification Protocol Guide (Kapa Biosystems, Wilmington, MA, catalog no. KK4854) and qualified using the TapeStation D1000 ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, catalog no. 5067-5582). Indexed libraries were then submitted to an Illumina NovaSeq (Illumina), and the paired-end (2 × 100 bp) sequencing was performed by Macrogen (Seoul, Republic of Korea).
RNA-seq data analysis
FastQC version 0.11.7 was used for quality control of RNA-seq reads. Adaptor clipping and sequence quality trimming were performed using Trimmomatic version 0.38.
36
Bases with a base quality <3 from read ends, and bases that do not qualify window size of 4 or mean quality of 15 were removed. Bases with a minimum length shorter than 36 bp were then removed to create the final trimmed data. Preprocessed reads were mapped to the reference genome (mm10) using HISAT2 version 2.1.0, Bowtie2 2.3.4.1 aligner to create aligned reads. StringTie version 2.1.3b was used to assemble transcripts from the aligned reads. Novel transcript assembly was excluded using the –e option. Read counts were normalized to fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads and transcripts per kilobase million by transcript length and sequencing depth coverage. Data were normalized by applying the trimmed mean of M-values normalization method using the calcNormFactors in the edgeR library. The DEGs were identified using the limma R package. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was performed to create adjusted
p
values and the false discovery rate (FDR). Genes with FDR <0.05 were considered to be differentially expressed.
Tissue genomic DNA extraction and WGBS
Twelve tissue samples created as previously described were used for WGBS. Genomic DNA was extracted from tissue samples by using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit (Qiagen). Prior to library preparation, DNA were quantified using the Quant-iT PicoGren dsDNA Assay Kit (Invitrogen) and measured by Victor Nivo (PerkinElmer, Hopkinton, MA). The WGBS libraries were prepared using the Accel NGS Methyl Seq DNA library kit (Swift BioSciences, Ann Arbor, MI). Briefly, 200 ng genomic DNA was sheared using adaptive focused acoustic technology Covaris to a target peak size of 300–400 bp. The fragmented DNA was then subject to bisulfite conversion using the EZ DNA Methylation Gold Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The final libraries were quantified using qPCR according to the qPCR Quantification Protocol Guide (KAPA Library Quantification kits for Illumina sequencing platforms) and qualified using the TapeStation HSD1000 ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies). Sequences were performed using the Nova Seq (Illumina) by Macrogen.
WGBS data processing
Trimming was performed using Trim Galore 0.5.0. Bases 18 bp each from the 3′ ends of R1 and the 5′ ends of R2 were trimmed, and reads with lengths <20 bp were dropped to produce clean data. Alignment of the cleaned reads to the reference genome (
Mus musculus
mm10), de-duplication, and methylation calling were performed using BSMAP version 2.90. The evaluation of the quality of the alignment data was performed with Qualimap 2.2. Methylation ratios of every single cytosine satisfying higher than 1 C+T count in the locus were called using methyratio.py in BSMAP. For further analysis, CpG outside the lower read cutoff of 10 and the higher read cutoff of 500 were excluded. Methylation levels over the whole genome were quantified using BSMAP with recommended parameters, and the methylation ratio values were normalized using median scaling normalization methods. To identify differential methylation regions (DMRs) between the SCA7 mice and WT mice, statistical analysis using the absolute mean methylation difference value of two groups per comparison pair was performed. DMR was defined as absolute mean methylation difference >0.2.
Sample preparation for proteomics analysis
Whole-brain tissue samples were collected from SCA7
266Q/5Q
mice and their WT littermates at week 12 (
n
= 6 per group). Tissues were lysed in protein extraction buffer, including 4% SDS, 2 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP), and 0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 7.5. Lysates were sonicated and heated for 30 min at 95°C. After centrifugation at 15,000 rpm for 10 min to remove insoluble materials, the concentration of proteins was measured using a reducing agent-compatible bicinchoninic acid assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). Then, each sample containing 200 μg total protein was precipitated with 5 volumes of cold acetone. Samples were re-suspended in denaturation buffer (2% SDS, 10 mM TCEP, 50 mM chloroacetamide, and 0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 8.5) and heated for 15 min at 95°C. The proteins were digested via multistep digestion filter-aided sample preparation according to our previously described process.
37
After samples were loaded onto a 30-K spin filter, UA buffer (8 M urea in 0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 8.5) was added to the filter. Buffer exchanges were performed with UA solution twice and 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate solution three times by centrifugation. The first protein digestion was performed at 37°C overnight using trypsin/LysC (Promega, Madison, WI; protein-to-protease ratio = 100:1). The digested peptides were collected to a new collection tube by centrifugation. In the second digestion, the remaining proteins in the filter were digested at 37°C for 3 h using trypsin (protein-to-protease ratio = 1,000:1). Then, the digested peptides were collected by centrifugation, and an additional elution step was subsequently performed with 100 μL 50 mM HEPES, pH 8.5.
TMT labeling and desalting
Tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling was applied according to the manufacturer’s protocol, with some modifications.
37
Briefly, the TMT reagent (0.8 mg) was dissolved in 100% acetonitrile (ACN). After spiking with 500 ng peptides derived from ovalbumin as an internal standard, 25 μL of the reagent was added to 20 μg peptide samples along with ACN to give a final concentration of 30% (v/v). In WT mice, male samples were labeled with the tags TMT-127N, TMT-128N, and TMT-129N, whereas female samples were labeled with the tags TMT-130C, TMT-131N, and TMT-131C. In mutant mice, the same labeling strategy was also used. To merge two TMT experiments, pooled samples were labeled with TMT-126 in both samples. After incubation at room temperature (25°C) for 1 h, the reaction was quenched with 15.3 μL 5% hydroxylamine. TMT-labeled samples were pooled at a 1:1:1:1:1:1:1 ratio. The resulting peptide mixtures were vacuum centrifuged to dry and subjected to OASIS HLB solid-phase extraction (Waters, Milford, MA).
Offline high pH reversed-peptide fractionation for deep coverage
The TMT-labeled peptide mixtures were subjected to high-pH peptide reversed-phase fractionation using Agilent 1290 bioinert high-performance liquid chromatography (Agilent Technologies) equipped with an analytical column (4.6 μm × 250 mm, 5 μm). Solvent A consisted of 15 mM ammonium hydroxide in water, and solvent B consisted of 15 mM ammonium hydroxide in 90% ACN. The peptides were separated with a gradient of 5%–35% ACN at a flow rate of 0.2 mL/min. In total, 96 fractions were non-continuously pooled into 24 fractions.
38
The fractions were lyophilized and stored at −80°C until mass spectrometry (MS) analysis.
MS and data processing
The 24 peptide fractions were analyzed with an liquid chromatography (LC)-MS system (Orbitrap Exploris 480, Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with an Ultimate 3000 RSLC system (Dionex, Sunnyvale, CA) via EASY-Spray LC columns as the electrospray source, and the temperature of the column heater was set to 60°C. Peptides were separated on a 2-column system with a trap column (3 mm diameter and 1 cm length) and an analytic column (75 μm diameter and 50 cm length) using 0.1% formic acid in water as solvent A and 0.1% formic acid in 80% ACN as solvent B. The samples were separated using a 180-min gradient from 7% to 32% solvent B at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. The survey MS scans were acquired in the range of 350–1650
m/z
with a resolution of 120,000 at 200
m/z
. Data acquisition was operated in the data-dependent mode using a top 20 method to select up to 20 of the most abundant precursor ions with an isolation width of 0.7
m/z
. High-energy collisional dissociation scans were acquired with a normalized collision energy of 32 and a resolution of 30,000 at 200
m/z
. The maximum ion injection times for the survey scan and tandem MS (MS/MS) scan were 25 and 85 ms, respectively.
Raw MS/MS files were processed with Proteome Discoverer version 2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), using the SEQUEST HT algorithms against the Human Uniprot protein sequence database (December_2019). The database search parameters were as follows: full enzyme digest using trypsin (after KR/-), with up to two missed cleavages allowed; a precursor ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm; a fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.02 Da; dynamic modifications of 15.995 Da for methionine oxidation and 42.011 Da for protein N-terminal acetylation; and static modifications of 57.021 Da for carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues and 229.153 Da for TMT 6-plex on any N terminus. The MS1 co-isolation threshold was set to 50%. Six reporter ion intensities for TMT were corrected for isotopic impurities as provided by the manufacturer. Peptide spectral matches and peptides were confirmed by a Percolator based on a 1% FDR. Confidence criteria were set to a 1% FDR at the protein level.
Proteomic data analysis
Pre-processing and statistical analysis of proteomic data were performed using Perseus software (version 1.6.15.0).
39
Protein expression levels were estimated by determining the logarithmic (log2(x)) intensities of the TMT-reporter ions. Valid values were filtered using proteins with quantified values in all TMT sets. After quantile normalization, the batch effect among the two TMT 7-plex sets was eliminated using the IRS algorithm.
40
The Student’s t test controlled by a permutation-based FDR <0.05 was applied for the identification of the DEPs.
Integration of RNA-seq, WGBS, and proteomics data
RNA-seq analysis results were matched with WGBS results to combine gene expression profiles with methylation status. DEGs with logFC values >1.5 and an absolute mean methylation difference lower than −0.2 were filtered and considered to be significantly hypomethylated-upregulated. DEGs with logFC values smaller than −1.5 and absolute mean methylation difference larger than 0.2 were considered to be significantly hypermethylated-downregulated. Cluster analyses of the matched DEGs were performed based on the logFC values. Matched DEGs were also visualized using a Starburst plot created using GraphPad Prism software version 9.3.1. GO enrichment analysis of the matched DEGs was performed using the TCGAbiolinks R package. Matched gene expression data were then compared with proteomic analysis results to identify DEGs, leading to significant alteration of protein expression. Thus, DEGs with matching DEPs were identified and called DEGs of interest.
Collection of public datasets and their analysis
Expression profiles of the three DEGs of interest (
Fam107b
,
Tph2
, and
Gpr88
) in other SCA mouse models were analyzed using publicly open datasets of SCA1 and SCA2 mice. For the SCA1 dataset, cerebellar RNA-seq data of the ATXN1 transgenic mice (
ATXN1
[
82Q
]
,
ATXN1
[
30Q
]
D776
) and control mice at week 12 were retrieved from the literature (GEO:
GSE75778
).
13
For the SCA2 dataset, cerebellar RNA-seq data of the ATXN2
Q127
mice and control mice at week 6 was retrieved from the literature (GEO: PRJEB24319).
14
Results of the differential analysis were extracted from available data, and interesting genes were selected and visualized by GraphPad Prism 9.3.1.
RNA extraction and qPCR
Mouse brain tissues were dissected from SCA7 mice and their WT littermates at week 12 (
n
= 4, each) to quickly freeze in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) after homogenization utilizing TissueLyser 2 (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA was prepared using 1 μg total RNA with PrimeScript RTase (TaKaRa, Kusatsu, Japan) and oligodT primer (TaKaRa). Diluted cDNA and 10 pmol primers (
Table S2
) were mixed with PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA). qPCR was performed under the thermal cycling program consisting of 95°C for 2 min for enzyme activation, followed by 40 cycles of 95°C for 15 s, 60°C for 15 s, and 72°C for 30 s (Applied Biosystems). Relative quantification using the 2-ΔΔCT method
41
was analyzed to observe the FC of target gene expression.
body:
Introduction
Spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 (SCA7) is a form of autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia (ADCA) with clinical phenotypes of cerebellar dysfunction and retinal degeneration.
1
,
2
Excessive prolongation of CAG repeat sequence in the
Atxn7
gene was discovered to be the cause in 1997, with larger repeat size correlating with earlier onset.
3
,
4
SCA7 patients suffer from various cerebellar symptoms such as dysarthria, gait ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia, as well as extracerebellar symptoms, eventually leading to death within 2–3 decades.
1
,
2
,
3
Retinal degeneration progresses in patients with early onset before the 5
th
decade of life, leading to visual impairment.
2
,
3
Recent advances in molecular science have led to a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms that contribute to neurodegeneration in SCA7. Studies have shown that gene dysregulation plays a key role in pathogenesis, along with defects in other pathways such as mitochondrial function and autophagy.
5
,
6
Deficits in the transcriptional and epigenetic levels have been proposed to lead to gene dysregulation. At the transcriptional level, dysfunction of the Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase (SAGA) complex, an important transcriptional coactivator of RNA polymerase II, is thought to be one of the essential contributing factors.
7
,
8
ATXN7 is a core component of the SAGA complex, and in SCA7 patients, mutant ATXN7 fragment aggregates can lead to SAGA complex dysfunction by sequestration of its key components.
9
Mechanisms independent of the SAGA complex have also been proposed to contribute to gene dysregulation through alterations in the function of RAR-related orphan receptor α, CREB binding protein, and histone deacetylase 3.
5
Epigenetic changes can also be found in mutant ATXN7-expressing cells and SCA7 mouse models.
8
,
10
,
11
,
12
Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing studies in SCA7 mice cerebella and photoreceptors have uncovered significant alterations in the acetylation of different gene promoters.
11
,
12
Differences in the level of histone H2B, presumed to result from defects in deubiquitination, are also reported.
9
It can be inferred from these significant changes in transcriptional and epigenetic profiles that disturbances in gene regulation may impact the expression of downstream protein expression, which ultimately leads to neurodegeneration and manifestation of clinical phenotypes in SCA7. However, there are no available data on the proteomic profiles of SCA7 models.
Therefore, we implemented a multi-omics approach to describe the transcriptomic, epigenetic, and proteomic profile of entire brain tissue in fully symptomatic SCA7
266Q/5Q
mice. The primary objective was to provide a thorough illustration of gene expression profiles in a stepwise manner and to integrate the findings to discover key genes worth further investigation. Validation of the dysregulation of key genes was performed by quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (RT-qPCR), and analysis of open-source data was performed to examine the significance of the key genes in other polyglutaminergic ADCAs. Through this process, we aimed to discover core genes that play fundamental roles in pathogenesis, which may be important targets for future treatment development.
Results
Behavioral test results
Behavioral tests, including stride length measurement and rotarod tests, were performed in SCA7
266Q/5Q
mice (SCA7 mice) and their wild-type (WT) littermates at weeks 7, 9, and 11 to validate replicability of clinical phenotypes (
Figure 1
A). A total of 12 SCA7 mice (male = 6, female = 6) and 7 WT mice (male = 3, female = 4) completed the full length of tests. The average stride length showed no difference between SCA7 mice and WT mice at week 7 (SCA7 vs. WT: 53.5 vs. 60.8 mm,
p
= 0.079), but progressively decreased in SCA7 mice at week 9 (SCA7 vs. WT: 52.2 vs. 69.8 mm,
p
< 0.001) and week 11 (SCA7 vs. WT: 41.9 vs. 54.5 mm,
p
= 0.036) (
Figure 1
B). In the rotarod tests, the average latency to fall showed no difference between SCA7 mice and WT mice at week 7 (SCA7 vs. WT, day 1: 208.8 vs. 173.1 s,
p
= 0.113; day 2: 239.8 vs. 232.4 s,
p
= 0.633; day 3: 216.3 vs. 240.5 s,
p
= 0.270), but progressively decreased in the SCA7 mice to show significant differences from the WT mice in week 9 (SCA7 vs. WT, day 1: 189 vs. 262 s,
p
< 0.001; day 2: 199.0 vs. 241.7 s,
p
= 0.011; day 3: 166.3 vs. 274.7 s,
p
< 0.001) and in week 11 (SCA7 vs. WT, day 1: 133.7 vs. 243.1 s,
p
< 0.001; day 2: 144.6 vs. 234.6 s,
p
< 0.001; day 3: 139.7 vs. 256.3,
p
< 0.001) (
Figure 1
C). Thus, clinical phenotypes of progressive motor incoordination are well represented in the SCA7 mice and were evident after week 9.

Matching of transcriptomic and epigenetic profiles and GO enrichment analysis
To gain insight into transcriptional dysregulations in SCA7, we performed bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) profiling on the whole-brain tissue of SCA7 mice and their WT littermates at week 12 of age, after motor symptom manifestation. Using the same samples, we also performed whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) to analyze DNA methylation patterns and matched the results with transcriptomic data. A total of 491 genes were differentially expressed in the SCA7 mice compared with the WT, 220 genes were significantly upregulated, and 271 were significantly downregulated. Matching with methylation analysis revealed 58 significantly hypomethylated-upregulated genes and 62 hypermethylated-downregulated genes, which were selected for further analysis (
Table 1
). Cluster analysis of the matched differentially expressed genes (DEGs) showed a distinct expression pattern between the two groups (
Figure 2
A). Additionally, a starburst plot illustrated the genes with concordant results in both differential mRNA expression and methylation patterns (
Figure 2
B).

Discussion
We conducted a multi-omics analysis, encompassing transcriptomic, methylation, and proteomic profiles of SCA7
266Q/5Q
mice brains, and identified two genes through integrated data analysis:
Fam107b
and
Tph2
. Both genes were significantly downregulated and hypermethylated, resulting in lower protein expression in SCA7 mice compared to WT. Moreover, we validated our results with an alternative method and investigated the importance of identified genes in other polyglutaminergic ADCAs using open-source data.
Our multi-omics study is of the largest scale to date performed in SCA7 mouse models and will serve as an important reference for future studies on the pathogenesis and endeavors to discover novel therapeutic approaches. Previous studies separately described the transcriptomic profiles and difference in acetylation patterns of SCA7 mice, but data from these studies cannot be fully integrated due to differences in methodology.
11
,
12
,
15
,
16
Our study is significant in that it encompasses the methylation patterns and proteomic analysis of whole-brain tissues of SCA7 mice with full-blown behavior symptoms.
The two genes we discovered,
Fam107b
and
Tph2
, showed consistent results across transcriptomic, epigenetic, and proteomic analyses. Concordant matching among the three pathways demonstrates that these genes may play direct roles in disease pathogenesis. They could play causative roles or may be core molecules in the downstream of key pathways.
Fam107b
is involved in corticogenesis, neuronal migration and layering during development, and cerebellar plasticity.
17
,
18
,
19
Although it is unclear from our results how mutant
Atxn7
affects corticogenesis, it seems fairly certain that downregulation of
Fam107b
and its final resulting protein occurs during the process, and it is consistent with previous studies as well.
Fam107b
was one of the strongest downregulated Purkinje cell-specific genes in SCA7
140Q/5Q
knockin mice cerebellum.
15
Fam107b
was also significantly downregulated in Purkinje cells of SCA
266Q/5Q
mice at week 8.5, analyzed by single-nucleus RNA-seq.
16
In other ADCAs, regulation profiles of
Fam107b
showed conflicting results in SCA1, when comparing our data with open-source data and previous study results.
5
,
13
However, for SCA2, all data consistently demonstrated the downregulation of
Fam107b
, similar to our findings in SCA7.
14
,
15
,
20
Consistent deregulation among different types of SCAs suggests a need to investigate further its potential as a treatment target. Future studies may be designed to see whether reversal of
Fam107b
downregulation leads to the rescue of clinical phenotypes.
Tph2
encodes tryptophan hydroxylase 2, which is an enzyme responsible for the generation of 5-hydroxytryptophan mainly in the brainstem of vertebrates, the first step in the serotonin (5-HT) synthesis pathway.
21
In the CNS, serotonin functions as a neurotransmitter and is related to mood disorders and regulation of the sleep cycle.
22
,
23
,
24
,
25
Mice with functional mutations or complete lack of this gene show postnatal growth retardation and behavioral changes such as increased anxiety.
22
In humans, while there are no transcriptomic studies of brain tissue, people with >10 CAG trinucleotide repeats in
Atxn7
show a higher lifetime odds ratio of suffering from depression compared with those with ≤10 repeats.
26
Also, SCA7 patients commonly experienced sleep-related symptoms such as insomnia.
27
Historically, numerous efforts have been made to modulate the serotonergic system to treat cerebellar ataxia patients.
28
,
29
,
30
,
31
,
32
Drugs such as buspirone, a 5-HT1A agonist, and ondansetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist, have shown partial effect in improving symptoms in randomized clinical trials. While these practices were not based on solid evidence and largely relied on clinical observations, so far our study provides indirect evidence for these endeavors. Additionally, previous study results that confirmed the downregulation of
Tph2
in SCA1 and SCA2 mouse models further strengthens the importance of this particular gene.
13
,
14
It will be interesting for future studies to observe whether supplementation of serotonin in SCA7 mouse models from an early stage leads to differences in their disease course.
Our study has some limitations. Due to methodological issues of bulk RNA-seq, it is not clear to which cell types the differences in gene expression can be attributed. Also, by analyzing whole-brain tissue, direct comparison with previous transcriptomic studies is difficult, where mostly only cerebellar tissue was analyzed. Pooling of samples can introduce bias or omission of certain DEGs. Moreover, differences in expression may merely be a downstream effect of other key molecules, and further study is needed to confirm the biological significance and therapeutic potential of the identified genes. Future studies could analyze the chronological expression pattern of the described molecules in different stages of disease or may observe the effects of restoring dysregulation to normal levels by methods such as implanting cDNA. Further investigation based on our data may reveal novel targets that could serve as potential biomarkers or therapeutic targets.
Conclusion
In this multi-omics analysis study of SCA7 mouse brain, we identified two genes,
Fam107b
and
Tph2
, that showed dysregulation across the levels of gene expression, methylation, and protein expression. Further studies are required to validate their biological significance and potential as treatment targets.
Materials and methods
The SCA7 mouse model
The SCA7
266Q/5Q
mice used in this study carry a 266 CAG repeat knockin in the exon 3 of the
Atxn7
locus, and replicate well the clinical features of infantile SCA7 (JAX stock no. 008682).
33
For healthy controls, B6.129S1 WT littermates were used. All procedures in animal handling were conducted with the approval of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Seoul National University Hospital (no. 22-0035-S1A1).
Behavioral tests
As behavioral tests, average stride length measurement and rotarod tests were performed. Twelve SCA7 mice (male = 6, female = 6) and 7 WT mice (male = 3, female = 4) were tested at weeks 7, 9, and 11 after birth. For average stride length measurement, each mouse performed two trials for every measurement period, and the average length of three strides was calculated. For the rotarod test, mice underwent four trials each on three sequential days for every measurement time point. For each trial, rotation speed was accelerated from 4 to 50 rpm, and trials were separated by 10 min each. The average latency to fall was measured and analyzed as the index parameter. All procedures were performed according to standardized protocols by experienced researchers. Statistical analysis was performed using the Student’s t test for difference in stride length, and we used multiple unpaired t tests for latency to fall in the rotarod test, correcting for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Šídák method. The overall procedure is depicted in
Figure 1
A.
Total RNA extraction, library preparation, and sequencing
Tissue collection of entire brain (including cerebrum and cerebellum) was performed on 24 mice at week 12 (
n
= 12 per group). Entire brain was selected as the target for analysis, considering that the cortex and brainstem are also regions significantly affected in SCA7,
33
and to obtain an overview of the genes that have the most general impact in overall pathogenesis. Twelve samples were created by pooling two samples from mice of matching genotype and sex. Pooling of samples was conducted to compensate for potential within-group variability.
34
,
35
Total brain RNA was extracted using QIAzol Lysis Reagent (Qiagen, Crawley, UK) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The total RNA concentration was calculated by Quant-IT RiboGreen (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, catalog no.
R11490
). To assess the integrity of the total RNA, samples were run on the TapeStation RNA screentape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, catalog no. 5067-5576). Only high-quality RNA preparations, with RNA integrity number >7.0, were used for RNA library construction. A library was independently prepared with 1 μg total RNA for each sample by Illumina TruSeq Stranded mRNA Sample Prep Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, catalog no. 20020595). The libraries were quantified using KAPA Library Quantification kits for Illumina sequencing platforms according to the qPCR Quantification Protocol Guide (Kapa Biosystems, Wilmington, MA, catalog no. KK4854) and qualified using the TapeStation D1000 ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, catalog no. 5067-5582). Indexed libraries were then submitted to an Illumina NovaSeq (Illumina), and the paired-end (2 × 100 bp) sequencing was performed by Macrogen (Seoul, Republic of Korea).
RNA-seq data analysis
FastQC version 0.11.7 was used for quality control of RNA-seq reads. Adaptor clipping and sequence quality trimming were performed using Trimmomatic version 0.38.
36
Bases with a base quality <3 from read ends, and bases that do not qualify window size of 4 or mean quality of 15 were removed. Bases with a minimum length shorter than 36 bp were then removed to create the final trimmed data. Preprocessed reads were mapped to the reference genome (mm10) using HISAT2 version 2.1.0, Bowtie2 2.3.4.1 aligner to create aligned reads. StringTie version 2.1.3b was used to assemble transcripts from the aligned reads. Novel transcript assembly was excluded using the –e option. Read counts were normalized to fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads and transcripts per kilobase million by transcript length and sequencing depth coverage. Data were normalized by applying the trimmed mean of M-values normalization method using the calcNormFactors in the edgeR library. The DEGs were identified using the limma R package. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was performed to create adjusted
p
values and the false discovery rate (FDR). Genes with FDR <0.05 were considered to be differentially expressed.
Tissue genomic DNA extraction and WGBS
Twelve tissue samples created as previously described were used for WGBS. Genomic DNA was extracted from tissue samples by using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit (Qiagen). Prior to library preparation, DNA were quantified using the Quant-iT PicoGren dsDNA Assay Kit (Invitrogen) and measured by Victor Nivo (PerkinElmer, Hopkinton, MA). The WGBS libraries were prepared using the Accel NGS Methyl Seq DNA library kit (Swift BioSciences, Ann Arbor, MI). Briefly, 200 ng genomic DNA was sheared using adaptive focused acoustic technology Covaris to a target peak size of 300–400 bp. The fragmented DNA was then subject to bisulfite conversion using the EZ DNA Methylation Gold Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The final libraries were quantified using qPCR according to the qPCR Quantification Protocol Guide (KAPA Library Quantification kits for Illumina sequencing platforms) and qualified using the TapeStation HSD1000 ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies). Sequences were performed using the Nova Seq (Illumina) by Macrogen.
WGBS data processing
Trimming was performed using Trim Galore 0.5.0. Bases 18 bp each from the 3′ ends of R1 and the 5′ ends of R2 were trimmed, and reads with lengths <20 bp were dropped to produce clean data. Alignment of the cleaned reads to the reference genome (
Mus musculus
mm10), de-duplication, and methylation calling were performed using BSMAP version 2.90. The evaluation of the quality of the alignment data was performed with Qualimap 2.2. Methylation ratios of every single cytosine satisfying higher than 1 C+T count in the locus were called using methyratio.py in BSMAP. For further analysis, CpG outside the lower read cutoff of 10 and the higher read cutoff of 500 were excluded. Methylation levels over the whole genome were quantified using BSMAP with recommended parameters, and the methylation ratio values were normalized using median scaling normalization methods. To identify differential methylation regions (DMRs) between the SCA7 mice and WT mice, statistical analysis using the absolute mean methylation difference value of two groups per comparison pair was performed. DMR was defined as absolute mean methylation difference >0.2.
Sample preparation for proteomics analysis
Whole-brain tissue samples were collected from SCA7
266Q/5Q
mice and their WT littermates at week 12 (
n
= 6 per group). Tissues were lysed in protein extraction buffer, including 4% SDS, 2 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP), and 0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 7.5. Lysates were sonicated and heated for 30 min at 95°C. After centrifugation at 15,000 rpm for 10 min to remove insoluble materials, the concentration of proteins was measured using a reducing agent-compatible bicinchoninic acid assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). Then, each sample containing 200 μg total protein was precipitated with 5 volumes of cold acetone. Samples were re-suspended in denaturation buffer (2% SDS, 10 mM TCEP, 50 mM chloroacetamide, and 0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 8.5) and heated for 15 min at 95°C. The proteins were digested via multistep digestion filter-aided sample preparation according to our previously described process.
37
After samples were loaded onto a 30-K spin filter, UA buffer (8 M urea in 0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 8.5) was added to the filter. Buffer exchanges were performed with UA solution twice and 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate solution three times by centrifugation. The first protein digestion was performed at 37°C overnight using trypsin/LysC (Promega, Madison, WI; protein-to-protease ratio = 100:1). The digested peptides were collected to a new collection tube by centrifugation. In the second digestion, the remaining proteins in the filter were digested at 37°C for 3 h using trypsin (protein-to-protease ratio = 1,000:1). Then, the digested peptides were collected by centrifugation, and an additional elution step was subsequently performed with 100 μL 50 mM HEPES, pH 8.5.
TMT labeling and desalting
Tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling was applied according to the manufacturer’s protocol, with some modifications.
37
Briefly, the TMT reagent (0.8 mg) was dissolved in 100% acetonitrile (ACN). After spiking with 500 ng peptides derived from ovalbumin as an internal standard, 25 μL of the reagent was added to 20 μg peptide samples along with ACN to give a final concentration of 30% (v/v). In WT mice, male samples were labeled with the tags TMT-127N, TMT-128N, and TMT-129N, whereas female samples were labeled with the tags TMT-130C, TMT-131N, and TMT-131C. In mutant mice, the same labeling strategy was also used. To merge two TMT experiments, pooled samples were labeled with TMT-126 in both samples. After incubation at room temperature (25°C) for 1 h, the reaction was quenched with 15.3 μL 5% hydroxylamine. TMT-labeled samples were pooled at a 1:1:1:1:1:1:1 ratio. The resulting peptide mixtures were vacuum centrifuged to dry and subjected to OASIS HLB solid-phase extraction (Waters, Milford, MA).
Offline high pH reversed-peptide fractionation for deep coverage
The TMT-labeled peptide mixtures were subjected to high-pH peptide reversed-phase fractionation using Agilent 1290 bioinert high-performance liquid chromatography (Agilent Technologies) equipped with an analytical column (4.6 μm × 250 mm, 5 μm). Solvent A consisted of 15 mM ammonium hydroxide in water, and solvent B consisted of 15 mM ammonium hydroxide in 90% ACN. The peptides were separated with a gradient of 5%–35% ACN at a flow rate of 0.2 mL/min. In total, 96 fractions were non-continuously pooled into 24 fractions.
38
The fractions were lyophilized and stored at −80°C until mass spectrometry (MS) analysis.
MS and data processing
The 24 peptide fractions were analyzed with an liquid chromatography (LC)-MS system (Orbitrap Exploris 480, Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with an Ultimate 3000 RSLC system (Dionex, Sunnyvale, CA) via EASY-Spray LC columns as the electrospray source, and the temperature of the column heater was set to 60°C. Peptides were separated on a 2-column system with a trap column (3 mm diameter and 1 cm length) and an analytic column (75 μm diameter and 50 cm length) using 0.1% formic acid in water as solvent A and 0.1% formic acid in 80% ACN as solvent B. The samples were separated using a 180-min gradient from 7% to 32% solvent B at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. The survey MS scans were acquired in the range of 350–1650
m/z
with a resolution of 120,000 at 200
m/z
. Data acquisition was operated in the data-dependent mode using a top 20 method to select up to 20 of the most abundant precursor ions with an isolation width of 0.7
m/z
. High-energy collisional dissociation scans were acquired with a normalized collision energy of 32 and a resolution of 30,000 at 200
m/z
. The maximum ion injection times for the survey scan and tandem MS (MS/MS) scan were 25 and 85 ms, respectively.
Raw MS/MS files were processed with Proteome Discoverer version 2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), using the SEQUEST HT algorithms against the Human Uniprot protein sequence database (December_2019). The database search parameters were as follows: full enzyme digest using trypsin (after KR/-), with up to two missed cleavages allowed; a precursor ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm; a fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.02 Da; dynamic modifications of 15.995 Da for methionine oxidation and 42.011 Da for protein N-terminal acetylation; and static modifications of 57.021 Da for carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues and 229.153 Da for TMT 6-plex on any N terminus. The MS1 co-isolation threshold was set to 50%. Six reporter ion intensities for TMT were corrected for isotopic impurities as provided by the manufacturer. Peptide spectral matches and peptides were confirmed by a Percolator based on a 1% FDR. Confidence criteria were set to a 1% FDR at the protein level.
Proteomic data analysis
Pre-processing and statistical analysis of proteomic data were performed using Perseus software (version 1.6.15.0).
39
Protein expression levels were estimated by determining the logarithmic (log2(x)) intensities of the TMT-reporter ions. Valid values were filtered using proteins with quantified values in all TMT sets. After quantile normalization, the batch effect among the two TMT 7-plex sets was eliminated using the IRS algorithm.
40
The Student’s t test controlled by a permutation-based FDR <0.05 was applied for the identification of the DEPs.
Integration of RNA-seq, WGBS, and proteomics data
RNA-seq analysis results were matched with WGBS results to combine gene expression profiles with methylation status. DEGs with logFC values >1.5 and an absolute mean methylation difference lower than −0.2 were filtered and considered to be significantly hypomethylated-upregulated. DEGs with logFC values smaller than −1.5 and absolute mean methylation difference larger than 0.2 were considered to be significantly hypermethylated-downregulated. Cluster analyses of the matched DEGs were performed based on the logFC values. Matched DEGs were also visualized using a Starburst plot created using GraphPad Prism software version 9.3.1. GO enrichment analysis of the matched DEGs was performed using the TCGAbiolinks R package. Matched gene expression data were then compared with proteomic analysis results to identify DEGs, leading to significant alteration of protein expression. Thus, DEGs with matching DEPs were identified and called DEGs of interest.

RNA extraction and qPCR
Mouse brain tissues were dissected from SCA7 mice and their WT littermates at week 12 (
n
= 4, each) to quickly freeze in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) after homogenization utilizing TissueLyser 2 (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA was prepared using 1 μg total RNA with PrimeScript RTase (TaKaRa, Kusatsu, Japan) and oligodT primer (TaKaRa). Diluted cDNA and 10 pmol primers (
Table S2
) were mixed with PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA). qPCR was performed under the thermal cycling program consisting of 95°C for 2 min for enzyme activation, followed by 40 cycles of 95°C for 15 s, 60°C for 15 s, and 72°C for 30 s (Applied Biosystems). Relative quantification using the 2-ΔΔCT method
41
was analyzed to observe the FC of target gene expression.
